$description: Motion primitives — how long a thing takes, and the shape of the curve it takes it on. Duration used to live in typography.json, which was a filing accident rather than a decision; the CSS variable names are unchanged (--keel-duration-*) because the primitive/semantic grouping is stripped from the name, so this is a pure move. Easing is new: every transition in the system was previously written with the bare CSS `ease` keyword, which is a hardcoded value wearing a keyword's clothes — it cannot be re-tuned centrally and it is the same curve for a 120ms hover tint as for a 200ms knob travel, which are not the same motion problem.

instant.$description: No transition. Used by the reduced-motion path so the token, not a media query buried in a component, carries the decision.

fast.$description: Colour and opacity changes on hover and focus. Fast enough to feel like a direct response rather than an animation.

medium.$description: Anything that moves in space — a switch knob travelling, a disclosure opening. Position changes need longer than tint changes to read as motion rather than as a jump.

spin.$description: One full rotation of a busy indicator. A token rather than a local value because the system has two spinners — the Spinner component and the Button's inline loading ring — and they were running at 700ms and 600ms respectively. Nobody chose that; it is what happens when the same idea is written twice. They are now the same object at two sizes.

standard.$description: The default. Leaves fast and settles slowly, which reads as a physical object coming to rest. Use for anything the user did not directly drag.

entrance.$description: Decelerate-only. For something arriving on screen — a popover, a toast. Starting at full speed and slowing makes the arrival feel like it was already in motion rather than starting from nothing.

exit.$description: Accelerate-only. For something leaving. Deliberately quicker off the mark than `entrance` is: a user who has dismissed something has already stopped caring about it, and easing it out slowly reads as lag.

overshoot.$description: Travels past its target and settles back. Reserved for a control the user has just thrown a switch on — the overshoot is what makes a toggle feel mechanical rather than animated. Use it nowhere else: on content it reads as a bug, and on anything larger than a knob it reads as seasick.
